name: Treating acid reflux for voice

lead: People with chronic hoarseness or frequent throat clearing are sometimes evaluated for laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR, or silent reflux) and treat it to get a clearer voice.

LPR is the backward flow of stomach contents into the throat, thought to irritate the larynx and cause hoarseness and strain. Many patients have little or no heartburn. Trials of acid-suppressing drugs for LPR have shown mixed results, and the diagnosis itself is debated.

paras: Management commonly combines diet and lifestyle changes, medication such as proton-pump inhibitors, alginate products, and sometimes surgery, usually guided by a clinician.
Hoarseness has many causes, and clinicians generally recommend evaluation when it persists. PPIs have their own adverse-effect profiles, and long-term use warrants clinician involvement.

angle.text: Controlling reflux reduces irritation of the larynx, which can ease hoarseness and give a clearer voice. Treatment studies for LPR are mixed and the diagnosis is debated.

lead: Treating acid reflux for voice refers to managing laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR), sometimes called silent reflux, with the aim of relieving hoarseness and improving voice quality. LPR is the backward flow of stomach contents into the larynx, oropharynx or nasopharynx.[1]

Hoarseness is considered a primary symptom of LPR and can lead to vocal strain and fatigue, and may progress to muscle tension dysphonia that can persist after reflux is controlled.[1] Many patients have little or no heartburn.[1]

Management commonly combines lifestyle measures, proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs) and alginate products. Evidence for PPIs in LPR is described as mixed to disappointing, and the diagnosis itself is debated.[1]

paras: LPR is often treated as a subtype of GERD but is described as having a different pathophysiology and symptom profile. Throat clearing occurs in about 87% of LPR cases compared with fewer than 5% of GERD cases, while heartburn appears in about 20% versus over 80%.[1]

Symptoms are nonspecific, and laryngoscopic findings such as redness and swelling have been found in many people without symptoms. Questionnaires such as the Reflux Symptom Index, laryngoscopy and pH monitoring are used.[1]

Lifestyle measures listed include avoiding chocolate, caffeine, acidic and fatty foods, weight loss, quitting smoking, limiting alcohol, and not eating shortly before bed. PPIs are the most common medication, alginates form a foam barrier, and fundoplication surgery may be offered when medical management fails.[1]

Vocal-hygiene programs address reflux alongside allergies as non-speech factors affecting the voice, and voice therapy from a speech-language pathologist may be needed for persistent strain.[2][1] Reinke's edema is another voice condition for which reflux control is part of first-line management.[3]

Studies of PPIs for LPR have been mixed. A 2006 trial of esomeprazole for chronic posterior laryngitis is cited as showing a disappointing response, and a 2008 review reported many studies finding PPIs no more effective than placebo for LPR.[1] A 2017 meta-analysis found alginate therapy effective for GERD symptoms, and a review covered voice outcomes in 1,483 patients.[1] The Wikipedia entry itself flags several PPI statements as disputed. A 2022 NHS approval of an oral training device was based on tentative evidence from uncontrolled trials.[1]
